title: A cut cable disrupted hundreds of flights across the US
summary: Construction crews in New Jersey accidentally cut a Verizon fiber cable used for air traffic control, causing hundreds of flights to be cancelled or delayed across the Northeast. The outage resulted in ground stops at all three major New York City airports, while Verizon blamed construction contractors and claimed no responsibility for the incident.
content:
A JetBlue airplane past an FAA air traffic control tower at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, US, on Friday, Oct. 24, 2025. JetBlue Airways Corp. is expected to release earnings figures on October 28. Photographer: Ryan Collerd/Bloomberg via Getty Images | Bloomberg via Getty Images	

Hundreds of flights were cancelled or delayed on Monday after construction crews in New Jersey accidentally cut a Verizon fiber cable used for air traffic control. 
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that a circuit failure led to the discovery of the severed fiber cable, ABC News reports. The outage hammered airports across the Northeast, causing ground stops at all three major New York City airports.
In a statement to CNBC, Verizon said that it bore "no responsibility for this incident," putting the blame on "construction contractors working in the area" that "dug up and cut our cable."

title: Amazon wants to help the Colorado River, but we still don’t know how much water the company uses
summary: Amazon announced a $20 million investment in water conservation projects along the Colorado River as part of its goal to become water positive by decade's end. However, the company has not fully disclosed its total data center water consumption, leaving questions about its actual environmental impact.
content:
Amazon plans to spend $20 million on water conservation projects along the Colorado River, a crucial but dwindling water supply for 40 million people in the Western US. 
The initiative comes as Amazon and other tech companies face mounting scrutiny over how much water their data centers use. Amazon has a goal of becoming water positive - replenishing more water than it uses - by the end of the decade. It recently disclosed some information about its water use, but we still have an incomplete picture of the company's impact as a whole.
Amazon announced the launch of a Colorado River Basin Collaborative today, with a mission to "create one o …

title: California tightens rules on AI data center energy and water use
summary: California Governor Gavin Newsom signed legislation requiring AI data centers to pay for grid and water system upgrades while disclosing their resource consumption to local governments. The bills establish new rate classifications for data centers and mandate energy efficiency and drought planning requirements. These regulations aim to prevent utilities from passing infrastructure costs onto residents.
content:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed seven bills designed to prevent AI data centers from passing utility costs onto residents, as reported earlier by the Los Angeles Times. The package of laws requires the California Public Utilities Commission to introduce a new rate classification for data centers, while forcing them to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems.
Other bills included in the package will require proposed data centers to disclose their estimated water use to local governments, along with information about energy efficiency and drought planning. They must also meet certain energy, water, and fuel consumption …

This suggests strong early market acceptance for Meta's AI agent offering. The comparison highlights shifting user preferences in the mobile AI assistant market.

title: GM can’t ‘bring back’ Apple CarPlay because it never left
summary: General Motors announced updated software for upcoming trucks featuring new Apple CarPlay and Android Auto implementations, leading to headlines claiming GM was "bringing back" these features it removed in 2023. However, GM clarified it never removed CarPlay from gas-powered vehicles, only from certain electric models. The confusion reflects how selective media coverage can distort corporate product strategy narratives.
content:
Last week, GM announced a new software experience for its upcoming Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks, including a new look for Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, the popular phone mirroring systems that the automaker made a big deal about removing from its electric vehicles in 2023. 
Naturally, this led to some confusion about whether GM was "bringing back" CarPlay and Android Auto to its vehicles. Yahoo Finance reported it that way, calling it an "about-face" by the automaker, while Apple Insider's headline boasted that GM "cave[d]" on its decision to remove the interface from its gas-powered vehicles. Even The Verge's own commenters were …

This deal paves the way for one of media's largest consolidations.

Paramount has reached a settlement with California and the 11 other states that sued to block its planned $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The settlement removes a major roadblock standing in the way of the massive media merger.
According to the proposed consent decree filed with the court, it includes requirements like minimum numbers of theatrical film releases over the next five years, starting with 30 in year one and two, and 32 in the following years, and a commitment to spend at least $300 million more on production in the US compared to what the companies spent in 2025. content: A third-party cybersecurity firm accidentally gave experimental Gemini models access to the Internet.

title: Bungie says it’s ‘not done with Destiny’ and will bring back vaulted content
summary: Bungie announced it will restore previously removed content from Destiny 2, reversing its controversial 2020 Destiny Content Vault decision that deleted campaigns, destinations, and raids players had purchased. The studio acknowledges the policy damaged player trust and is working to rebuild goodwill. This marks a significant strategic reversal following years of player criticism.
content:
Months after seemingly giving up on Destiny 2, Bungie now says it's planning to restore vaulted content in the game like campaigns, destinations, and raids. The decision reverses the Destiny Content Vault that Bungie created six years ago, controversially removing older content from Destiny 2 that players had paid to access.
"We understand that removing these experiences had a lasting impact on player trust and enjoyment of Destiny," admits Bungie. "We cannot change the decision we made, but we can acknowledge its impact and do the work to make it right by restoring these important parts of Destiny's history."

title: Grab an Xbox controller and a $50 Xbox gift card together for just $80

The wireless controller features Bluetooth connectivity, a headphone jack, and swappable batteries, making it compatible with Xbox, PC, and gaming handhelds.
content:
Newegg is hosting a bundle that includes Microsoft’s wireless Xbox controller (in black) and a $50 digital Xbox gift card together for $80. Given that this model typically sits around $50 to $60 depending on the color you want, this is a fantastic value since it essentially knocks its price down to $30. Another way of thinking about it is you’re paying full price for the controller, but getting a big discount on the gift card.
Xbox Wireless Controller

Where to Buy:

 $80 at Newegg (with $50 gift card)

The controller included is a great option for Xbox or for PC. It supports Bluetooth connectivity, and it’s also a solid wireless gamepad to connect to a Steam Deck or any other gaming handheld that can be docked to a TV. While it lacks Hall effect sticks, it’s the best midrange controller from Microsoft yet, with a premium-feeling, comfortable design, a headphone jack, and good battery life (it supports swappable AA batteries).

title: Can John Ternus find Apple’s next big thing?
summary: Bloomberg's chief Apple correspondent Mark Gurman discusses new CEO John Ternus's first major product launch, the iPhone Duo foldable smartphone, and how his leadership signals Apple's shift from the iPhone era into the AI era.
content:
Today, I’m talking with Mark Gurman, who is the world’s best-sourced Apple reporter — both as Bloomberg’s chief Apple correspondent and the host of the upcoming podcast Power On. 
Earlier this month, Apple hosted its annual iPhone hardware event, virtually every detail of which was reported ahead of time by Mark. But this event was special, for a number of reasons. 
It was new Apple CEO John Ternus’ first major product launch since he took over for former CEO Tim Cook less than two weeks prior. It was also the debut of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable smartphone. The timing of those two things was not at all coincidental, as you’ll hear Mark explain. Apple takes these hardware events — and the stories they tell — extremely seriously. 
This year’s story actually says a great deal about what’s happening at Apple, how Cook managed in wholesale leadership ranks over the past year, and how all of that might change Apple’s culture. Furthermore, what all that tells about Ternus’ plan to navigate Apple from what you might call the iPhone era into the AI era.
Okay: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman on the future of Apple. Here we go.


This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. 
Mark Gurman, you’re the chief Apple correspondent and the managing editor of consumer technology at Bloomberg. Welcome to Decoder.
Good to be here finally. Thanks for having me. And it’s been a while, so it’s good to catch up on all things Apple.
Yeah, I’m really excited to talk to you. Obviously, Apple just had its big event. They announced the iPhone Duo. It was John Ternus’s first event as CEO. This is a Decoder episode, so we’ve got a new CEO, and we’ve got a new org chart inside of Apple.
There’s been a lot of shuffling. You’ve been chronicling them very, very deeply over the past few years. Let’s just start with the event. I have a very basic question for you.
Sure.
Do you ever get nostalgic for a time when you didn’t know what was going to happen at the iPhone event?

title: Get a closer look at the iPhone 18 Pro’s mechanical camera
summary: iFixit's teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro reveals Apple's new variable aperture lens features hair-thin magnetic blades that control light exposure while fitting in the same camera footprint as last year's model. The teardown also surfaces potential repair concerns for users and technicians.
content:
Each of those teeny lens blades is around the same thickness as a human hair. | Image: iFixit	

iFixit's latest device teardown shows us the inner workings of the new variable aperture lens inside Apple's iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, alongside some repair concerns to be mindful of. The adjustable mechanical iris opens and closes magnetically, controlling how much light should pass through to the sensor, featuring six leaf-like overlapping blades that are each about as thin as a human hair.

title: UN says AI safeguards can’t wait for certainty
summary: A UN scientific panel warned that governments must implement AI safeguards before the technology's full risks are understood, elevating AI safety as a critical global diplomatic priority. The assessment reflects concerns over increasingly capable AI agents amid ongoing US-China AI negotiations.
content:
The United Nations logo at the UN headquarters in New York. | Getty Images	

Governments need to rein in increasingly capable AI agents before their risks are fully understood, a United Nations scientific panel warned in the global organization's first major assessment of OpenAI's hack of Hugging Face earlier this year.
The report cements AI's place on the global diplomatic agenda this week as leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly and the US and China hold talks on AI. Last week, UN secretary general António Guterres called on governments to cooperate on addressing the threats posed by AI, warning that "the world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety."

title: Amazon doesn’t trust Meta’s Muse AI agent
summary: Amazon blocked Meta's Muse AI agent from shopping on its platform, citing unauthorized access and security concerns including the agent's failure to identify itself and potential customer credential exposure. The incident highlights growing friction between AI agent developers and e-commerce security protocols.
content:
Meta's Muse AI agent has been blocked from shopping Amazon on behalf of its users, GeekWire reports. A popup message started appearing on Sunday for Muse users saying that "continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed."
According to GeekWire, Meta didn't notify Amazon that Muse would access its store. Amazon also expressed privacy and security concerns over Muse failing to identify itself when it browses, and seemingly capturing customer credentials.
